hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, for example astrocytes, APOE4 causes impaired ARF6-related recycling of receptors between the cell surface and the endosome, compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: Surface biotinylation in three biological replicates showed approximately 50% lower plasma-membrane LRP1 in APOE4 than APOE3 astrocytes.
rows.Finding quote: First, surface biotinylation revealed that plasma membrane expression of LRP1 receptor in ApoE4 astrocytes was lower by ∼50% ( Fig. 2 B ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower surface LRP1 in astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse astrocyte cultures from ApoE-knockout mice with isogenic human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in, supplied by David Holtzman; age and strain not stated; cell-surface biotinylation and LRP1 immunoblotting, with Na+/K+-ATPase as loading control.

rows.Finding description: Live-cell surface-antibody flow cytometry in three biological replicates showed approximately 55% fewer surface-LRP1-positive cells in APOE4 than APOE3 astrocyte cultures.
rows.Finding quote: Second, an antibody directed against an external epitope of LRP1 to quantify surface expression in live cells by flow cytometry analysis showed a reduction of LRP1-positive cells by ∼55% in ApoE4 astrocytes ( Fig. 2 C ) and by ∼51% in patient-derived ApoE4/4 fibroblasts ( SI Appendix , Fig. S2 D ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower fraction of surface-LRP1-positive astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse astrocyte cultures from ApoE-knockout mice with isogenic human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in, supplied by David Holtzman; age and strain not stated; external-epitope LRP1 antibody labeling of live, nonpermeabilized cells on ice followed by flow cytometry; 10,000 cells per experimental sample according to Fig 2C.

rows.Finding description: Surface-antibody confocal microscopy showed approximately 49% lower LRP1 labeling in APOE4 than APOE3 astrocytes.
rows.Finding quote: Third, this was confirmed by confocal microscopy showing ∼49% lower LRP1 surface labeling by antibody in ApoE4 ( Fig. 2 D ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower surface LRP1 immunofluorescence in astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse astrocyte cultures from ApoE-knockout mice with isogenic human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in, supplied by David Holtzman; age and strain not stated; live-cell external-epitope LRP1 labeling on ice, followed by fixation, secondary-antibody staining, and confocal microscopy.

rows.Finding description: Confocal microscopy showed less LRP1 on astrocyte processes and greater perinuclear LRP1 accumulation in APOE4 than APOE3 cells.
rows.Finding quote: Confocal microscopy revealed a striking loss of LRP1 from astrocyte processes and increased perinuclear accumulation in ApoE4 cells, relative to ApoE3 ( Fig. 2 F ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower process-associated and higher perinuclear LRP1 in astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse astrocyte cultures from ApoE-knockout mice with isogenic human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in, supplied by David Holtzman; age and strain not stated; LRP1 immunofluorescence examined by confocal microscopy, including enlarged regions and orthogonal sections.

rows.Finding description: Restoring NHE6 expression in APOE4 astrocytes increased surface LRP1 immunofluorescence approximately 2.5-fold compared with empty-vector controls.
rows.Finding quote: Compared with the weak surface LRP1 staining in vector-transfected ApoE4 astrocytes, we observed prominent, ∼2.5-fold higher LRP1 staining in ApoE4 cells expressing ectopic NHE6 ( Fig. 4 F ).
rows.Finding summary: (empty vector -> NHE6 expression in APOE4 astrocytes) -> (higher surface LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse astrocyte cultures from ApoE-knockout mice with human APOE4 knock-in, supplied by David Holtzman; age and strain not stated; lentiviral NHE6-GFP expression versus empty vector; surface LRP1 immunofluorescence in nonpermeabilized cells measured by confocal microscopy; post-transduction interval not stated.

rows.Finding description: The normalized LRP1 internalization assay in three biological replicates found no significant difference between APOE4 and APOE3 astrocytes after 10 minutes at 37 °C.
rows.Finding quote: No difference in LRP1 internalization was observed between ApoE3 and ApoE4 astrocytes (p=0.2112; n=3; Student’s t-test).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (no change in normalized LRP1 internalization)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse astrocyte cultures from ApoE-knockout mice with isogenic human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in, supplied by David Holtzman; age and strain not stated; surface LRP1 antibody labeling on ice, 10-minute incubation at 37 °C versus 4 °C, and flow-cytometric measurement of remaining surface label to calculate normalized internalization.

rows.Finding description: Restoring NHE6 expression in APOE4 astrocytes increased surface-biotinylated LRP1 approximately 5.7-fold compared with empty-vector controls.
rows.Finding quote: Similar results were obtained in surface biotinylation experiments that showed robust, ∼5.7-fold higher surface LRP1 levels in ApoE4 cells with restored NHE6 expression, compared with transfection with empty vector ( SI Appendix , Fig. S7 C ).
rows.Finding summary: (empty vector -> NHE6 expression in APOE4 astrocytes) -> (higher surface LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse astrocyte cultures from ApoE-knockout mice with human APOE4 knock-in, supplied by David Holtzman; age and strain not stated; lentiviral NHE6-GFP expression versus empty vector followed by surface biotinylation and LRP1 immunoblotting; total LRP1 was measured alongside surface LRP1.

rows.Finding description: Restoring NHE6 expression in APOE4 astrocytes reduced perinuclear LRP1 accumulation and partially restored LRP1 staining on astrocyte processes.
rows.Finding quote: Consistent with these findings, confocal microscopy revealed a reduction in perinuclear accumulation of LRP1 and partial restoration of staining on astrocyte processes in ApoE4 cells with NHE6 expression ( SI Appendix , Fig. S7 E ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE4 control -> NHE6 expression in APOE4 astrocytes) -> (lower perinuclear and higher process-associated LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse astrocyte cultures from ApoE-knockout mice with human APOE4 knock-in, supplied by David Holtzman; age and strain not stated; NHE6 expression followed by LRP1 immunofluorescence and confocal microscopy, with APOE3 astrocytes shown as a localization reference.

rows.Finding description: TSA treatment of APOE4 astrocytes increased surface LRP1 approximately twofold compared with vehicle treatment in three biological replicates.
rows.Finding quote: Importantly, we observed prominent, approximately twofold higher surface LRP1 expression in ApoE4 cells with TSA treatment ( Fig. 5 E and SI Appendix , Fig. S8 G ).
rows.Finding summary: (vehicle -> TSA in APOE4 astrocytes) -> (higher surface LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse astrocyte cultures from ApoE-knockout mice with human APOE4 knock-in, supplied by David Holtzman; age and strain not stated; TSA versus DMSO treatment; external-epitope LRP1 surface labeling at 4 °C and flow cytometry; dose and duration are not separately specified for this panel.

rows.Finding description: Surface-antibody flow cytometry during the LRP1 internalization assay showed lower LRP1 staining in APOE4 than APOE3 astrocytes.
rows.Finding quote: Note lower LRP1 staining in ApoE4 astrocytes, relative to ApoE3, due to reduced surface expression.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower surface LRP1 staining during the internalization assay)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse astrocyte cultures from ApoE-knockout mice with isogenic human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in, supplied by David Holtzman; age and strain not stated; extracellular LRP1 antibody labeling on ice followed by 10 minutes at 4 °C or 37 °C, detection of remaining surface antibody, and flow cytometry.

rows.Finding description: A ligand-binding assay performed on ice showed 66% lower surface-bound fluorescent amyloid in APOE4 than APOE3 astrocytes, providing a surrogate for available surface amyloid receptors.
rows.Finding quote: In a fourth approach, surface-bound ligand (fluorescent Aβ) measured by confocal microscopy was 66% lower in ApoE4 astrocytes ( Fig. 2 E ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower surface amyloid binding in astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse astrocyte cultures from ApoE-knockout mice with isogenic human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in, supplied by David Holtzman; age and strain not stated; fluorescent Aβ surface binding for 10 minutes on ice followed by washing, fixation, and confocal microscopy; this measures surface ligand binding rather than clearance.

rows.Finding description: Flow cytometry of three biological replicates showed approximately 1.5-fold higher steady-state transferrin uptake in APOE4 than APOE3 astrocytes, an indirect readout that does not distinguish increased internalization from reduced recycling.
rows.Finding quote: In contrast, cell-associated TFN was 1.5–twofold higher in ApoE4 cells relative to ApoE3 as measured by flow cytometry ( Fig. 1 D ) and confocal microscopy ( Fig. 1 E ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher steady-state cell-associated transferrin in astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse astrocyte cultures from ApoE-knockout mice with isogenic human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in, supplied by David Holtzman; age and strain not stated; fluorescent transferrin uptake for 60 minutes measured by flow cytometry; approximately 10,000 cells analyzed per biological replicate.

rows.Finding description: Confocal microscopy showed approximately twofold higher steady-state cell-associated transferrin in APOE4 than APOE3 astrocytes, without separately measuring receptor recycling.
rows.Finding quote: In contrast, cell-associated TFN was 1.5–twofold higher in ApoE4 cells relative to ApoE3 as measured by flow cytometry ( Fig. 1 D ) and confocal microscopy ( Fig. 1 E ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher steady-state transferrin accumulation in astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse astrocyte cultures from ApoE-knockout mice with isogenic human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in, supplied by David Holtzman; age and strain not stated; one-hour fluorescent transferrin uptake measured by confocal microscopy with identical acquisition settings and background subtraction.

rows.Finding description: Flow cytometry showed approximately 1.93-fold higher transferrin uptake in APOE4/4 Alzheimer’s patient fibroblasts than age-matched APOE3/3 control fibroblasts, without resolving receptor recycling.
rows.Finding quote: Quantification of FACS analysis showing ∼1.93-fold increase in transferrin (TFN) uptake in ApoE4/4 fibroblasts, relative to ApoE3/3 control (****p=5.9X10-7; n=3; Student’s t-test).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3/3 control -> APOE4/4 Alzheimer’s patient fibroblasts) -> (higher transferrin uptake)
rows.Experimental system: Human primary fibroblasts from Coriell: APOE3/3 control AG04387 and age-matched APOE4/4 Alzheimer’s patient AG10788; different donors, not isogenic; numerical ages not stated; 60-minute fluorescent transferrin uptake measured by flow cytometry.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: At 0.125 mg, full-length apoE–DMPC reduced bound ³H-LDL by 39–42% across the two isoforms. The authors described no overall isoform specificity. They gave no dose-specific significance test.
rows.Finding quote: The full-length apoE proteins with DMPC showed dose-de- pendent competing ability, whereas a 2.5-fold dose of apoE-DMPC complex lowered 39–42% of the bound 3H-LDL and 20-fold dose low- ered 81–83% (Fig. 5
rows.Finding summary: Full-length apoE3 and apoE4 showed similar observed LDLR competition at 0.125 mg with DMPC.
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; recombinant human full-length apoE expressed in E. coli with a C-terminal His tag, complexed with DMPC; 0.125 mg competitor; cells serum-starved for 24 h, then incubated with 3H-LDL and competitor at 4 °C for 2 h; cell-associated radiolabel measured. Brain cells, affinity constants, endosomal dissociation and receptor recycling were not examined.

rows.Finding description: With DMPC, Table 4 reports interpolated ³H-LDL binding reductions of 59% for full-length apoE3 and 58% for apoE4. ApoE4 had 99% of apoE3’s normalized LDLR binding ability. The authors described no isoform specificity and supplied no between-isoform significance test.
rows.Finding quote: The LDL-R binding ability of apoE- DMPC was higher than that of LDL at the same dose (20-fold), although apoE with or without DMPC did not show isoform specificity.
rows.Finding summary: Full-length apoE4 retained 99% of apoE3’s reported LDLR binding ability with DMPC.
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; E. coli-expressed, C-terminally His-tagged human full-length apoE; Table 4 reports 0.5 mg protein with 0.5 mg DMPC. Full-length 0.5 mg responses were interpolated from 0.125 and 1 mg measurements; 3H-LDL competition at 4 °C for 2 h. No receptor-recycling assay.
rows.Data location: Table 4, ApoE3 and ApoE4 rows, With DMPC columns

rows.Finding description: Without DMPC, full-length apoE3 and apoE4 each decreased ³H-LDL binding by 34%. Table 4 gives apoE4 100% of apoE3’s normalized binding ability. The authors supplied no between-isoform significance test.
rows.Finding quote: The LDL-R binding ability of apoE- DMPC was higher than that of LDL at the same dose (20-fold), although apoE with or without DMPC did not show isoform specificity.
rows.Finding summary: Full-length apoE3 and apoE4 gave identical reported LDLR competition without DMPC.
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; 0.5 mg E. coli-expressed, C-terminally His-tagged human full-length apoE without DMPC; 24 h serum starvation followed by competitive 3H-LDL binding at 4 °C for 2 h. No endosomal dissociation or receptor-recycling assay.
rows.Data location: Table 4, ApoE3 and ApoE4 rows, Without DMPC columns

rows.Finding description: ApoE4-(1–231)–DMPC competed more strongly for LDLR binding than apoE3-(1–231)–DMPC, decreasing 3H-LDL binding by 44% versus 18%.
rows.Finding quote: In contrast, the apoE3-(1–231)-DMPC complex lost most of its LDL-R binding abil- ity (31%), whereas that of apoE4-(1–231)-DMPC still maintained 75% of binding ability compared with the full-length apoE-DMPC (Table 4).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3-(1–231) -> apoE4-(1–231)) -> (greater LDLR competition with DMPC)
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; E. coli-expressed, C-terminally His-tagged human apoE-(1–231); 0.5 mg protein with DMPC; competitive 3H-LDL binding at 4 °C for 2 h. No receptor-recycling measurement.
rows.Data location: Fig 5B, bars 6 and 7; raw reductions in Table 4

rows.Finding description: Without DMPC, apoE4-(72–299) decreased 3H-LDL binding by 38%, whereas apoE3-(72–299) had a reported decrease of −8%, indicating competition only by the apoE4 fragment.
rows.Finding quote: On the contrary, in a lipid-free environment, the N-terminal trun- cated apoE4, especially apoE4-(72–299), showed equal or even higher LDL-R binding ability, compared with that of full-length apoE proteins, although the N-terminal truncated apoE3 showed lower or no LDL-R binding ability (Table 4).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3-(72–299) -> apoE4-(72–299)) -> (greater LDLR competition without DMPC)
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; 0.5 mg E. coli-expressed, C-terminally His-tagged human apoE-(72–299) without DMPC; competitive 3H-LDL binding at 4 °C for 2 h. No receptor-recycling assay.
rows.Data location: Table 4, ApoE3-(72–299) and ApoE4-(72–299) rows, Without DMPC columns

rows.Finding description: ApoE4-(72–299)–DMPC competed more strongly for LDLR binding than apoE3-(72–299)–DMPC, decreasing 3H-LDL binding by 34% versus 27%.
rows.Finding quote: At the same dose, apoE3-(72–299)- and apoE4-(72–299)-DMPC complexes showed only about half the 3H-LDL competing ability of full-length apoE (46 and 57%).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3-(72–299) -> apoE4-(72–299)) -> (greater LDLR competition with DMPC)
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; E. coli-expressed, C-terminally His-tagged human apoE-(72–299); 0.5 mg protein with DMPC; competitive 3H-LDL binding at 4 °C for 2 h. No endosomal dissociation or receptor-recycling assay.
rows.Data location: Fig 5A, bars 10 and 11; raw binding reductions in Table 4

rows.Finding description: ApoE4-(1–191)–DMPC competed less strongly for LDLR binding than apoE3-(1–191)–DMPC, decreasing 3H-LDL binding by 34% versus 42%.
rows.Finding quote: When the C-terminal domain was fully removed, apoE3-(1–191)- and apoE4-(1–191)-DMPC complexes still maintained 72 and 57% relative LDL-R binding ability, respectively (Table 4).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3-(1–191) -> apoE4-(1–191)) -> (lower LDLR competition with DMPC)
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; E. coli-expressed, C-terminally His-tagged human apoE-(1–191); 0.5 mg protein with DMPC; 3H-LDL competition measured after 2 h at 4 °C. No receptor-recycling measurement.
rows.Data location: Fig 5B, bars 4 and 5; raw reductions in Table 4

rows.Finding description: ApoE4-(1–271)–DMPC competed more strongly for LDLR binding than apoE3-(1–271)–DMPC, decreasing 3H-LDL binding by 58% versus 47%.
rows.Finding quote: With the assistance of the 232–271 fragment, the LDL-R binding ability of apoE3-(1–271)-DMPC was largely res- cued (80%) and that of apoE4-(1–271)-DMPC was fully recovered (99%; Table 4).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3-(1–271) -> apoE4-(1–271)) -> (greater LDLR competition with DMPC)
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; E. coli-expressed, C-terminally His-tagged human apoE-(1–271); 0.5 mg protein with DMPC; cell-associated 3H-LDL measured after competition at 4 °C for 2 h. No receptor-recycling measurement.
rows.Data location: Fig 5B, bars 8 and 9; raw reductions in Table 4

rows.Finding description: Without DMPC, apoE4-(1–191) produced greater LDLR competition than apoE3-(1–191), decreasing 3H-LDL binding by 19% versus 13%.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3-(1–191) -> apoE4-(1–191)) -> (greater LDLR competition without DMPC)
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; 0.5 mg E. coli-expressed, C-terminally His-tagged human apoE-(1–191) without DMPC; competitive 3H-LDL binding at 4 °C for 2 h. No receptor-recycling assay.
rows.Data location: Table 4, ApoE3-(1–191) and ApoE4-(1–191) rows, Without DMPC columns

rows.Finding description: At 0.5 mg competitor, apoE4-(41–299)–DMPC produced numerically greater LDLR competition than apoE3-(41–299)–DMPC, decreasing 3H-LDL binding by 47% versus 46%.
rows.Finding quote: A 10-fold dose of apoE3-(41–299)-DMPC complex decreased 3H-LDL binding by 46% and that of apoE4-(41–299)-DMPC complex decreased by 47% (Table 4).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3-(41–299) -> apoE4-(41–299)) -> (slightly greater LDLR competition with DMPC)
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; E. coli-expressed, C-terminally His-tagged human apoE-(41–299); 0.5 mg protein with DMPC; competitive cell-associated 3H-LDL binding measured at 4 °C after 2 h. No receptor-recycling measurement.
rows.Data location: Fig 5A, bars 8 and 9; numerical values also in Table 4

rows.Finding description: ApoE4-(72–166)–DMPC competed more strongly for LDLR binding than apoE3-(72–166)–DMPC, decreasing 3H-LDL binding by 55% versus 26%.
rows.Finding quote: Different from that of apoE3-(72–166)-DMPC, apoE4-(72–166)- DMPC complex showed very high efficiency in 3H-LDL competition.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3-(72–166) -> apoE4-(72–166)) -> (greater LDLR competition with DMPC)
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; E. coli-expressed, C-terminally His-tagged human apoE-(72–166); 0.5 mg protein with DMPC; competitive 3H-LDL binding at 4 °C for 2 h. No receptor-recycling measurement.
rows.Data location: Fig 5B, bars 10 and 11; raw reductions in Table 4

rows.Finding description: Without DMPC, apoE4-(41–299) produced numerically greater LDLR competition than apoE3-(41–299), decreasing 3H-LDL binding by 20% versus 15%.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3-(41–299) -> apoE4-(41–299)) -> (greater LDLR competition without DMPC)
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; 0.5 mg E. coli-expressed, C-terminally His-tagged human apoE-(41–299) without DMPC; competitive 3H-LDL binding measured at 4 °C for 2 h. No receptor-recycling assay.
rows.Data location: Table 4, ApoE3-(41–299) and ApoE4-(41–299) rows, Without DMPC columns

rows.Finding description: Without DMPC, apoE4-(1–271) produced numerically greater LDLR competition than apoE3-(1–271), decreasing 3H-LDL binding by 29% versus 27%.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3-(1–271) -> apoE4-(1–271)) -> (slightly greater LDLR competition without DMPC)
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; 0.5 mg E. coli-expressed, C-terminally His-tagged human apoE-(1–271) without DMPC; competitive 3H-LDL binding at 4 °C for 2 h. No receptor-recycling assay.
rows.Data location: Table 4, ApoE3-(1–271) and ApoE4-(1–271) rows, Without DMPC columns

rows.Finding description: Without DMPC, apoE4-(72–166) produced greater LDLR competition than apoE3-(72–166), decreasing 3H-LDL binding by 22% versus 14%.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3-(72–166) -> apoE4-(72–166)) -> (greater LDLR competition without DMPC)
rows.Experimental system: Human HepG2 hepatoblastoma cells; 0.5 mg E. coli-expressed, C-terminally His-tagged human apoE-(72–166) without DMPC; competitive 3H-LDL binding at 4 °C for 2 h. No receptor-recycling assay.
rows.Data location: Table 4, ApoE3-(72–166) and ApoE4-(72–166) rows, Without DMPC columns

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, for example astrocytes, APOE4 causes impaired ARF6-related recycling of receptors between the cell surface and the endosome, compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: APOE4 cells contained more transferrin immediately after loading. The normalized curves showed similar fractional recycling in the two genotypes. The paper reports six and three independent differentiations for pairs 1 and 2 and gives no significance test for the recycling-rate comparison.
rows.Finding quote: Similarly, the total amount of Tf after a 20-min pulse was higher in ApoE4 compared to ApoE3 iCE-BECs (Figure 6B), but the recycling rate was similar between the two genetic variants (Figure 6D).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher intracellular transferrin after loading; no change in fractional transferrin recycling in human iCE-BECs)
rows.Experimental system: Human iCE-BECs from the Bioni037 and Alstem homozygous APOE3/APOE4 isogenic pairs, assayed on differentiation day 14, three days after PECAM1 sorting. Cells received 25 µg/mL labeled transferrin for 20 minutes followed by 250 µg/mL unlabeled holo-transferrin for 0–60 minutes. Recycling curves were normalized to each condition immediately after the pulse.

rows.Finding description: Normalized transferrin pulse–chase curves showed similar recycling rates in APOE4 and APOE3 iCE-BECs. Pair 1 had six independent differentiations and pair 2 had three. The paper reports no genotype test for the fitted rates. ARF6 was not measured.
rows.Finding quote: Similarly, the total amount of Tf after a 20-min pulse was higher in ApoE4 compared to ApoE3 iCE-BECs (Figure 6B), but the recycling rate was similar between the two genetic variants (Figure 6D).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (no change in transferrin recycling rate in human iPSC-derived brain endothelial cells)
rows.Experimental system: Human iPSC-derived brain endothelial cells (iCE-BECs), day 14 of differentiation, from two homozygous APOE3/APOE4 isogenic pairs: Bioni037-A/Bioni037-A4 (healthy-donor fibroblast origin) and Alstem iPS26/iPS16 (bone marrow CD34-positive mononuclear cell origin). Cells received 25 µg/mL fluorescent transferrin for 20 minutes, followed by 250 µg/mL unlabeled holo-transferrin for 0–60 minutes; fixed-cell high-content confocal imaging measured transferrin fluorescence normalized to immediately after the pulse in each condition, with exponential fitting.

rows.Finding description: Live imaging of transferrin transport in isogenic human iPSC-derived brain endothelial cells showed frequent sorting-tubule formation and vesicle fission in APOE3 cells but reduced sorting-tubule formation in APOE4 cells.
rows.Finding quote: In agreement with previous data on mouse brain endothelial cells (Villaseñor et al., 2017), we observed frequent events of sorting tubule biogenesis and vesicle fission in ApoE3 iCE-BECs (Figure 5G; Videos S1 and S2). In contrast, the number of sorting tubules was substantially reduced in ApoE4 iCE-BECs (Figure 5H).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (reduced transferrin-positive sorting-tubule formation in human iCE-BECs)
rows.Experimental system: Human iPSC-derived brain endothelial cells (iCE-BECs), isogenic pair 1: homozygous APOE3 Bioni037-A (16423), originating from healthy-donor fibroblasts, versus its gene-edited homozygous APOE4 derivative Bioni037-A4 (I40-53); experiments performed on differentiation day 14 by default; incubated with 25 μg/mL Tf-Alexafluor488 for 3 h before live fluorescence imaging at 100×, acquiring 2 frames/s for 1 min.
rows.Data location: Fig 5G (representative events) and Fig 5H (genotype comparison of tubule formation)

rows.Finding description: Live imaging of isogenic pair 1 human iPSC-derived brain endothelial cells showed fewer transferrin-positive endosomal sorting tubules forming in APOE4 than APOE3 cells across three independent differentiations with 20 videos per experiment, providing a sorting surrogate without establishing ARF6 involvement.
rows.Finding quote: In contrast, the number of sorting tubules was substantially reduced in ApoE4 iCE-BECs (Figure 5H).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (reduced transferrin-positive endosomal sorting tubule formation in human iCE-BECs)
rows.Experimental system: Human iPSC-derived brain endothelial cells (iCE-BECs), isogenic pair 1: homozygous APOE3 Bioni037-A (16423), derived from a healthy individual's fibroblasts, versus homozygous APOE4 Bioni037-A4 (I40-53), generated by editing the parental APOE allele; donor age not stated. Experiments used day 14 cells under the default methods schedule. Cells were incubated with 25 μg/mL transferrin-Alexafluor488 for 3 h and imaged live for 1 min at 100×; two independent blinded raters manually counted sorting tubules, reported as formation events per 1,000 μm2 per minute.

rows.Finding description: Normalized continuous-uptake curves showed similar transferrin internalization rates in APOE4 and APOE3 iCE-BECs, with four independent differentiations for pair 1 and three for pair 2. The paper reports no pair-specific significance tests for the rates.
rows.Finding quote: However, the rate of Tf internalization was similar between ApoE4 and ApoE3 iCE-BECs (Figure 6C).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (no change in transferrin internalization rate in human iCE-BECs)
rows.Experimental system: Human iPSC-derived brain endothelial cells (iCE-BECs), homozygous APOE3 versus APOE4 in two isogenic pairs: Bioni037-A/Bioni037-A4, originating from healthy-donor fibroblasts, and Alstem iPS26/iPS16, originating from bone marrow CD34-positive mononuclear cells. At differentiation day 14, cells received 25 µg/mL fluorescent transferrin for 2–45 minutes; fixed-cell confocal imaging measured uptake kinetics, normalized to each condition's 10-minute intensity, with exponential curve fitting. This panel measured ligand internalization, an indirect readout for the hypothesized ARF6-related receptor recycling.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: At pH 4.5, PUFA-CE–lipidated ApoE4 formed more sedimentable aggregates than ApoE3 after four days at 37°C in a cell-free assay.
rows.Finding quote: Interestingly, CE(20:4)-ApoE3 demonstrated the lowest aggregation at both pH 7.4 and pH 4.5, while CE(20:4)-ApoE2 exhibited the highest aggregation at pH 7.4 but comparable aggregation as CE(20:4)-ApoE4 at pH 4.5 (Figure 5O–Q, Figure S5K).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (higher ApoE aggregation at lysosomal pH)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free HEK293-derived human ApoE lipidated with POPC and CE(20:4); 0.5 mg/mL protein in PBS adjusted to pH 4.5, four days at 37°C; ultracentrifugation at 150,000 × g for 30 minutes and non-reducing SDS-PAGE of supernatant and pellet.

rows.Finding description: Quantification across two PUFA-CE–ApoE preparation batches showed greater acidic-pH ApoE aggregation for ApoE4 than ApoE3, with variable absolute aggregation between batches.
rows.Finding quote: Interestingly, CE(20:4)-ApoE3 demonstrated the lowest aggregation at both pH 7.4 and pH 4.5, while CE(20:4)-ApoE2 exhibited the highest aggregation at pH 7.4 but comparable aggregation as CE(20:4)-ApoE4 at pH 4.5 (Figure 5O–Q, Figure S5K). Despite variability in the extent of aggregation across two independent batches of lipidated ApoE, the pH- and ApoE isoform-dependent aggregation of CE(20:4)-lipApoE was conserved.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (higher pelletable ApoE at lysosomal pH across preparation batches)
rows.Experimental system: Two independently prepared batches of HEK293-derived human CE(20:4)/POPC-lipidated ApoE; four-day incubation at 37°C and pH 4.5; ultracentrifugation followed by densitometry of the 34 kDa ApoE band.

rows.Finding description: Human astrocytes internalized more ApoE4 than ApoE3 after one day of lipidated ApoE treatment.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE isoform differences were manifested in the differential levels of internalized lipApoE (ApoE4 > ApoE3 > ApoE2), giving rise to the same isoform trend for LAMP1-positive vesicles containing ApoE immunoreactivity (Mander’s coefficients = 0.266 ± 0.045 for ApoE2, 0.410 ± 0.049 for ApoE3, 0.497 ± 0.090 for ApoE4) (Figure 2I).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (higher intracellular ApoE protein accumulation)
rows.Experimental system: Human APOE-knockout iPSC-derived astrocytes from ThermoFisher A18945; one-day treatment with 10 μg/mL HEK293-derived POPC-lipidated human ApoE; fixed-cell ApoE immunofluorescence with super-resolution imaging.

rows.Finding description: Internalized ApoE colocalized completely with LDLR for all three isoforms. ApoE–LAMP1 coefficients were similar for ApoE3 (0.903 ± 0.024) and ApoE4 (0.900 ± 0.008).
rows.Finding quote: Super-resolution imaging on APOE KO iAstrocytes confirmed internalized lipApoE completely colocalized with endogenous LDLR (Mander’s coefficient for ApoE puncta with colocalizing LDLR = 1 for all 3 isoforms), largely inside LAMP1 compartments (Figure 2H) (Mander’s coefficients for ApoE puncta with colocalizing LAMP1 = 0.823 ± 0.061 for ApoE2; 0.903 ± 0.024 for ApoE3; 0.900 ± 0.008 for ApoE4).
rows.Finding summary: (lipidated ApoE4 exposure) -> (predominantly lysosomal localization of internalized ApoE4)
rows.Experimental system: Human APOE-knockout iPSC-derived astrocytes generated from ThermoFisher A18945, originally APOE3/3; one-day treatment with 10 μg/mL POPC-lipidated ApoE4; ApoE, LDLR and LAMP1 immunostaining, Leica SP8 super-resolution imaging, ImageJ Coloc2.

rows.Finding description: At pH 7.4, PUFA-CE–lipidated ApoE3 showed less aggregation than ApoE4 after four days at 37°C, although the preparations remained largely soluble.
rows.Finding quote: CE(20:4)-lipApoE remained largely soluble and mostly recovered in the supernatant fraction upon incubation at pH 7.4, but abundant protein was found in the pellet fraction indicative of aggregation after incubation at pH 4.5, which mimics lysosomal pH (Figure 5O–P). Interestingly, CE(20:4)-ApoE3 demonstrated the lowest aggregation at both pH 7.4 and pH 4.5, while CE(20:4)-ApoE2 exhibited the highest aggregation at pH 7.4 but comparable aggregation as CE(20:4)-ApoE4 at pH 4.5 (Figure 5O–Q, Figure S5K).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (higher ApoE aggregation at neutral pH)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free HEK293-derived human ApoE3 or ApoE4 lipidated with POPC and CE(20:4); 0.5 mg/mL protein in PBS, pH 7.4, four days at 37°C; ultracentrifugation and non-reducing SDS-PAGE.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: Native-PAGE of non-AD human control CSF showed a lower apoE dimer/monomer ratio in APOE ε3/ε4 than ε3/ε3 samples (ratio D/M 0.38 versus 2.20, printed in the text).
rows.Finding quote: In the control group, the dimer/monomer quotient was significantly lower in the APOE ε3/ε4 group (ratio D/M = 0.38) compared to that of the ε3/ε3 group (ratio D/M = 2.20; p= 0.006), associated to the inability of the apoE4 isoform to form disulfide-linked dimers.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE ε3/ε3 -> APOE ε3/ε4) -> (lower CSF apoE dimer/monomer ratio)
rows.Experimental system: Human non-AD Gothenburg control lumbar CSF; APOE ε3/ε3 versus ε3/ε4; corresponding cohort mean ages 69±2 and 62±5 years; unheated native-PAGE and AB178479 immunoblotting. Bands were assigned as monomers and dimers using denatured CSF and recombinant apoE3 references. No cellular or endo-lysosomal localization was measured.
rows.Data location: Fig. 3D quantification; Fig. 3C representative native blots; Supplementary p. 7 complete source blots

rows.Finding description: Native-PAGE of human AD CSF showed a lower apoE dimer/monomer ratio in APOE ε4/ε4 than ε3/ε3 samples (ratio D/M 0.24 versus 2.27, printed in the text); the Fig. 3D bracket between these groups reads p < 0.0001.
rows.Finding quote: The same situation was found in the AD group, where the dimer/monomer ratio decreased as the ε4 allele was present (ε3/ε3: ratio D/M = 2.27; ε3/ε4: ratio D/M = 1.04; ε4/ε4: ratio D/M = 0.24).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE ε3/ε3 -> APOE ε4/ε4) -> (lower CSF apoE dimer/monomer ratio in AD)
rows.Experimental system: Human Gothenburg AD lumbar CSF, APOE ε3/ε3 versus ε4/ε4; corresponding cohort mean ages 79±2 and 73±1 years; unheated native-PAGE and AB178479 immunoblotting. Extracellular native apoE complexes were measured, without cell-type or compartment identification.
rows.Data location: Fig. 3D quantification; Fig. 3C representative native blots; Supplementary p. 7 complete source blots

rows.Finding description: Reducing SDS-PAGE of Gothenburg AD CSF showed significantly less approximately 100-kDa apoE-containing complex immunoreactivity in APOE ε4/ε4 than ε3/ε3 patients, with 15 patients per genotype.
rows.Finding quote: In the AD group, the 100-kDa apoE species levels were significantly lower in the APOE ε4/ε4 group when compared to both ε3/ε3 (p < 0.0001) and ε3/ε4 (p < 0.0001) groups.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE ε3/ε3 -> APOE ε4/ε4) -> (lower reducing-agent-resistant ~100-kDa CSF apoE complex abundance in AD)
rows.Experimental system: Human Gothenburg AD lumbar CSF, APOE ε3/ε3 versus ε4/ε4; 15 patients per genotype, mean ages 79±2 and 73±1 years; samples heated at 98°C for 5 minutes and analyzed by reducing SDS-PAGE and AB178479 immunoblotting, normalized to recombinant apoE3. No intracellular localization was measured.
rows.Data location: Fig. 4I quantification; Fig. 4A representative blot; Supplementary p. 8 complete source blots

rows.Finding description: Reducing SDS-PAGE of Barcelona AD CSF showed significantly less approximately 100-kDa apoE-containing complex immunoreactivity in nine APOE ε4/ε4 patients than in ten ε3/ε3 patients. Group values printed on the figure: Panel I printed medians: ε3/ε3 3.7 and ε4/ε4 2.8; approximately 24% lower in ε4/ε4; bracket p = 0.02.
rows.Finding quote: Within the AD group, the APOE ε4/ε4 samples once again displayed significantly lower 100-kDa apoE levels compared with ε3/ε3 cases (p = 0.02).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE ε3/ε3 -> APOE ε4/ε4) -> (lower reducing-agent-resistant ~100-kDa CSF apoE complex abundance in AD)
rows.Experimental system: Human Barcelona SPIN cohort AD lumbar CSF, APOE ε3/ε3 versus ε4/ε4; ten and nine patients, respectively, mean ages 75±2 and 72±2 years; heated reducing SDS-PAGE and AB178479 immunoblotting, normalized to recombinant apoE3. No intracellular localization was measured.
rows.Data location: Fig. 5I quantification; Fig. 5A representative blot; Supplementary p. 9 complete source blot

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: SEC profiling of control brain lysates showed a trend toward more large-sized soluble apoE in APOE4 carriers, but no significant difference from non-carriers was reported for the control comparison.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4 carriers showed a greater amount of larger size APOE protein (fraction #26 to #30) than APOE4 non-carriers, although the difference was not significant due to large sample-to-sample variations (Fig. 5e).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE4 non-carrier -> APOE4 carrier) -> (no change in large-sized soluble apoE reaching statistical significance in control brains)
rows.Experimental system: Human postmortem control superior temporal cortex from a brain bank; bulk tissue without identified cell types or endo-lysosomal localization. Control cohort APOE4 non-carriers had median age 82.5 years, range 79–91; carriers had median age 87 years, range 61–97. Ages and exact genotypes of the 4–5 SEC samples per group were not separately specified. TBS-soluble lysates underwent tandem Superose 6 SEC at pH 7.4 and apoE ELISA. Fig. 5d displays size distributions; the reported genotype comparison is summarized in Fig. 5e. ApoE molecular size does not establish endo-lysosomal aggregation.
rows.Data location: Fig. 5d; corresponding control fraction comparisons in Fig. 5e

rows.Finding description: Comparing control brain SEC fractions 26–30 showed no significant difference in large-sized soluble apoE between APOE4 carriers and non-carriers despite a higher trend in carriers, with 4–5 samples per group.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4 carriers showed a greater amount of larger size APOE protein (fraction #26 to #30) than APOE4 non-carriers, although the difference was not significant due to large sample-to-sample variations (Fig. 5e).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE4 non-carrier -> APOE4 carrier) -> (no change in large-sized soluble apoE reaching statistical significance in control brain fractions 26–30)
rows.Experimental system: Human postmortem control superior temporal cortex from a brain bank; bulk tissue with no specified cell type or organelle localization. Control cohort APOE4 non-carriers had median age 82.5 years, range 79–91; carriers had median age 87 years, range 61–97. Exact ages and genotypes of the 4–5 SEC samples per group were not separately reported. TBS-soluble lysates underwent tandem Superose 6 SEC at pH 7.4, followed by apoE ELISA and Student t tests. Larger apoE-containing species were measured without demonstrating apoE homo-oligomers or endo-lysosomal aggregates.

rows.Finding description: SEC followed by apoE ELISA showed more large-sized soluble apoE in fractions 27–29 in AD brains without LB pathology from APOE4 carriers than non-carriers, using six pooled samples per group.
rows.Finding quote: In AD cases without LB pathology, APOE4 carriers had more large-sized APOE (fractions #27-#29) compared to APOE4 non-carriers (Fig. 5a–c).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE4 non-carrier -> APOE4 carrier) -> (more large-sized soluble apoE in AD brains without LB pathology)
rows.Experimental system: Human postmortem superior temporal cortex from autopsy-confirmed AD cases without LB pathology, brain bank; bulk tissue, with no cell-type or endo-lysosomal localization. APOE4 non-carriers included APOE2/3 and APOE3/3; carriers included APOE2/4, APOE3/4, and APOE4/4. Respective cohort age medians were 81 and 83 years, with ranges 55–96 and 55–100; SEC-subset ages were not separately reported. Six samples per group, each pooling equal amounts of TBS lysate from 3–4 brains. Tandem Superose 6 SEC at pH 7.4 followed by apoE ELISA measured molecular-size distributions, without establishing whether larger species were apoE homo-oligomers or other apoE-containing complexes.
rows.Data location: Fig. 5a; Results, The presence of LB or APOE4 impacts the size distribution of APOE and α-SYN proteins

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: In three cell-free ELISA assays per group, apoE4 bound immobilized WT human LRP1 cluster IV more weakly than apoE3, with reported Kd values of 39.5 ± 3.2 versus 29.3 ± 2.1 nM, respectively.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (higher Kd and weaker binding to WT-LRPIV)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free binding ELISA using commercial apoE3 and apoE4 from Invitrogen and purified, untagged human WT-LRPIV expressed in CHO cells from a construct derived from human spleen RNA; immobilized receptor coating concentration 5 μg/ml; ligand incubation for 2 hours at room temperature in HBSC, pH 7.4, containing 0.05% Tween 20; apparent Kd fitted by nonlinear one-site binding regression. No brain cells or receptor recycling measurements.
rows.Data location: Table 3, APOE3 and APOE4 rows, WT-LRPIV Kd column

rows.Finding description: In three cell-free ELISA assays per group, apoE4 bound immobilized human LRP1 cluster IV mutant D3674G more tightly than apoE3, with reported Kd values of 49.9 ± 5.4 versus 54.3 ± 6.4 nM, respectively.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower Kd and stronger binding to LRPIV-D3674G)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free binding ELISA using commercial apoE3 and apoE4 from Invitrogen and purified human LRPIV-D3674G expressed in CHO cells; D3674G replaces an aspartate in the CR29 calcium-binding site; immobilized receptor coating concentration 5 μg/ml; ligand incubation for 2 hours at room temperature in HBSC, pH 7.4, containing 0.05% Tween 20; apparent Kd fitted by nonlinear one-site binding regression. No brain cells or receptor recycling measurements.
rows.Data location: Table 3, APOE3 and APOE4 rows, LRPIV-D3674G Kd column

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: In recombinant-protein experiments performed three times, PUFA-phospholipid incubation induced disulfide-linked ApoE3 dimerization but had no apparent effect on ApoE4 dimerization, opposing increased ApoE4 oligomerization under these cell-free conditions.
rows.Finding quote: Incubation with the PUFA-phospholipid PE-18:0/22:4n-6 had no apparent effect on ApoE4 dimerization (A). By contrast, incubation of ApoE3 (B) and ApoE2 (C) with PE-18:0/22:4n-6 produced prominent peaks with molecular weights corresponding to ApoE dimers and multimers, respectively.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (less PUFA-phospholipid-induced disulfide-linked apoE dimerization)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free recombinant human ApoE3 and ApoE4 incubated with PE-18:0/22:4n-6; protein separation and anti-ApoE immunodetection using the Jess automated capillary nano-immunoassay with chemiluminescence. DTT reversal supported disulfide dependence. Incubation duration and pH were not supplied; no brain cells or endosomal/lysosomal localization were examined.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: At one apoE molecule per particle, human E4/E4 LpB:E had a lower apparent LDLR dissociation constant than E3/E3 LpB:E, 9.1 versus 16.38±6 nM, indicating stronger binding; the E3/E3 value represented three preparations, whereas the E4/E4 preparation count was unstated.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4, one apoE per LpB:E particle) -> (lower apparent LDLR dissociation constant)
rows.Experimental system: Human HeLa cells, a non-brain carcinoma cell line of unspecified source, were preincubated for 48 hours with 10% lipoprotein-deficient serum. Human plasma LpB:E particles were isolated by sequential immunoaffinity chromatography from donors phenotyped E3/E3 or E4/E4; both preparations contained one apoB and one apoE per particle, without apoC-III. Direct iodine-125-labeled lipoprotein binding was measured at 4°C to avoid endocytosis, with a 20-fold excess of unlabeled LDL defining nonspecific binding. Apparent dissociation constants were calculated by Scatchard analysis. Receptor recycling was not measured.
rows.Data location: Table 2, LpB:E (n=3; apoE/apoB=1) and LpB E4/E4 rows
